prompt: An item originally priced at $\$200$ is discounted by $20\%$, and then an additional $10\%$ is taken off the sale price. What is the final price, in dollars?
hint: The second discount is taken from the sale price, not from the original price. That means the two percents cannot simply be added.

hints.text: The second discount is taken from the sale price, not from the original price. That means the two percents cannot simply be added.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try it on $\$100$: down $50\%$ gives $\$50$, then down $10\%$ of *that* gives $\$45$ — not $\$40$. The second discount applies to the reduced price, never to the original.
Taking $20\%$ off leaves $80\%$, so the sale price is $200 \times 0.80 = 160$. Then take $10\%$ off that by multiplying $160$ by $0.90$.
Since $160 \times 0.90 = 144$, the final price is $144$ dollars.

explanation: The first discount leaves $80\%$ of the price, so the sale price is $200 \times 0.80 = 160$ dollars.
The second discount applies to the sale price and leaves $90\%$ of it: $160 \times 0.90 = 144$.
Combining the multipliers gives the same result, since $200 \times 0.72 = 144$. The final price is $144$ dollars.

alternativeExplanations.title: A 30% discount is not the same thing
steps: Adding the two discounts suggests $30\%$ off, which would give a price of $140$ dollars, a tempting wrong answer.
The second discount is $10\%$ of the sale price of $160$ dollars, which is $16$ dollars, not $10\%$ of $200$.
The total taken off is $40 + 16 = 56$ dollars, a $28\%$ discount, so the final price is $200 - 56 = 144$ dollars.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Adding the discounts to get $30\%$ gives $140$ dollars, which is wrong because the $10\%$ acts on a price that is already reduced.
Chain the multipliers instead: $0.80 \times 0.90 = 0.72$, so the buyer pays $72\%$ of the original price.
That is $0.72 \times 200 = 144$ dollars, slightly more than the $140$ that adding the percents suggests.
